title: Victim loses £250k after scammers use AI video of 'well-known' celebrity

reading.body:
This is a synthetic-media impersonation fraud, not a failure of a model to answer a question. A generated video was used as the opening move in a longer confidence scheme, and the AI element sat at the top of the funnel, where it supplied the apparent endorsement that made the first payment plausible. Everything after that first payment was conventional fraud tradecraft: contact moved to WhatsApp, the victim was walked through opening accounts, remote access was taken, and borrowing was encouraged to keep the money flowing.

The failure mode is a fabricated endorsement presented as a real one. The video asserted, in the apparent voice and face of a public figure, that an investment existed and paid large returns. Nothing in the reporting establishes that any such investment existed, and the police account treats the endorsement itself as the deceptive instrument. Catching this at the point of harm would have required verifying the endorsement against its supposed source rather than against the video's own convincingness, and checking the counterparty against Financial Conduct Authority authorisation, which is the check the police later advised.

What is not established is who made the video, which celebrity was depicted, or whether any named figure had any connection to the scheme. The PSNI did not name the celebrity, and the similar cases the BBC saw involving other public figures are comparisons, not links to this one. The loss figure and the police characterisation come from a single report.

reports.title: Victim loses £250k after scammers use AI video of 'well-known' celebrity

summary:
A person in the Ards and north Down area lost £250,000 to an AI-generated scam. The victim saw a video that appeared to feature a well-known financial celebrity promoting an investment with large returns. After a small initial payment, fraudsters contacted the victim on WhatsApp and pushed for more money. They persuaded the victim to open multiple online accounts and gave them remote access to their computer, then encouraged borrowing to keep investing. The Police Service of Northern Ireland called it a sophisticated and substantial fraud.

The PSNI did not name the celebrity, though BBC News NI has seen similar scams using figures like Martin Lewis, Peter Jones and Steven Bartlett. Police said apparent celebrity endorsements do not prove an investment is real, and AI can create convincing videos, voices and endorsements. Superintendent Joanne Gibson urged people to stop and check financial activity and to talk with relatives about fraud. Police advised independently verifying who you deal with and checking Financial Conduct Authority authorisation.
title_en: Victim loses £250k after scammers use AI video of 'well-known' celebrity
